explain.say: Here is a puzzle: why is there nothing that hunts lions for food? Why don't food chains go on for ten or twenty links? The answer is all about energy. Let's work it out.

explain.say: Now watch these bars. Imagine the grass holds 10,000 units of energy. A zebra gets only about 1,000, a lion about 100, and the next level just 10. Each step keeps roughly a tenth. Can you see the bars shrinking?

See the fire? Most energy is not passed on. Animals use it to move, keep warm and stay alive, and it escapes as heat. And not everything gets eaten: roots, bones and droppings are left behind. Why does a running zebra pass on less?

faq.q: Where does the energy in a food chain come from?
faq.a: Almost all of it comes from sunlight, captured by producers in photosynthesis and stored as chemical energy in their bodies.
asks: Tell me about plants catching light

faq.q: How much energy passes to the next trophic level?
faq.a: On average only about 10%, though it can vary from about 5% to 20%. A trophic level is a feeding step, such as producer, herbivore or carnivore.

faq.q: Where does the rest of the energy go?
faq.a: Most is used for respiration, to power movement and keep warm, and is lost as heat. Some is in parts that are not eaten or not digested.
asks: Tell me about heat and movement

faq.q: Why isn't all of an animal eaten?
faq.a: Predators rarely eat bones, fur, hooves or roots, and some eaten food passes out undigested as droppings. That energy goes to decomposers instead.
asks: Tell me about what is not eaten

faq.a: So little energy reaches the top of a food chain that only a small number of top predators can be supported, and each one needs a big area to find enough food.
asks: Why are there so few tigers?

facts: On average about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next.
Most energy not passed on is released as heat during respiration.
